title: Memorizing chains
hook: students memorized chains and texts by heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women who carried hadith, and your line: she taught the sahih. Which name did you learn, and did you say it out loud to anyone? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

So-and-so told us, from so-and-so, from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ say. That's how the lesson begins, in a circle of students on a mosque floor, with no book open. Names first. Only then comes the saying itself. The students aren't listening for the saying alone. They're holding the names too, in order, because the names are how anyone will later know whether the saying can be trusted. Drop one link and the report limps. Swap two names and a careful critic will notice. Tradition tells of students who kept both, chain and text, in the one place no thief could reach. Today: memorizing chains.
screen: `NO BOOK OPEN.` → `NAMES FIRST, THEN THE SAYING.` → `KEPT WHERE NO THIEF COULD REACH.`

segments.voice: Start with the little word that did the heavy lifting: haddathana, he told us. In the collections it comes again and again, link after link. He told us, he told us, he told us. Each one is a person who sat in front of another person. To memorize a chain was to memorize a line of people. Next, why memory, when there was paper? Scholars wrote as well, and their notebooks mattered. But the two checked each other. A student who knew a report by heart could catch a copyist's slip, and a written page could catch a slip of memory. Then the reason underneath it all. In a report preserved by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet asks Allah to make radiant the face of a person who hears a saying from him, holds on to it, and passes it on. In another version, the person passes it on just as he heard it. Just as he heard it. That phrase sits under the whole enterprise, and it's why a narrator's memory was tested alongside his honesty. Last, this week, because today closes it. The four books of the Shia. The sacred hadith, where Allah speaks in the Prophet's phrasing. I am as My servant thinks of Me. Whoever comes walking, He comes running. Islam, iman and ihsan, taught in one scene. Women like Karimah, who taught the Sahih. Every one of those reached this lesson because a person held it carefully, often by heart, and handed it on just as it was heard.
screen: `HADDATHANA: HE TOLD US.` · `MEMORY AND PAPER CHECK EACH OTHER.` · `JUST AS HE HEARD IT.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS HELD BY HEART.`

segments.voice: The practice: memorize one short hadith. Here's one from Sahih Muslim, in plain English: religion is sincere counsel. Say it once, slowly. Close your eyes and say it again without looking. Now give it a simple chain: Muslim, from those before him, from Tamim al-Dari, from the Prophet. Say the chain, then the line. Then just sit with the line. When your mind wanders, bring it home with those four words. If you pray, you can hold it in your prayer today. The bell holds the time.
Memorizing chains. Holding the names of the narrators, in order, together with the words they carried, by heart. Today's word.

Your line: by heart. Today, say the line you memorized once aloud and once in silence, and check this evening whether it's still there. Tomorrow: weak hadith and virtue. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Students of hadith traditionally learn reports with their chains from a teacher, and many Muslims memorize short hadith, such as "religion is sincere counsel", as a way of keeping them close.

pairs: how a saying is to be passed on
from Sahih Muslim, through Tamim al-Dari

fork.setup: you're a student. your teacher has recited a report, and you realize you've lost one name in the middle of the chain. what do you do?
options: fill in the name that seems most likely.
go back, ask, and pass it on just as you heard it.
pass on the saying with no chain at all.
fork.reveal: the whole craft leans on passing it on just as you heard it. a guessed name is exactly what a critic would catch.

original.note: Arabic: guarding, keeping safe, and so learning by heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: memorizing chains sounds like a feat of trivia.
what it means: the names were carried with the words, so the words could be tested.
what a scholar hears: haddathana, he told us, link after link, and a prayer in al-Tirmidhi for whoever passes a saying on just as he heard it.

notes: Tirmidhi 2656 (Zayd ibn Thabit: hears, memorizes and conveys) and 2657 (Ibn Mas'ud: conveys it as he heard it), also Abu Dawud 3660: confirm numbers and that the paraphrases fit both versions.

Bukhari 1 (actions are only by intentions, narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab) is described as the 'opening' of the Sahih; confirm. The practice gives a deliberately simplified chain ('from those before him'); confirm this is acceptable for a beginner exercise.
'Haddathana' described as recurring link after link in the collections; other transmission terms (akhbarana, 'an) also occur. Confirm the simplification.
'Memory and writing checked each other' is a general description of the practice, with no dates or counts; confirm.
Week-end look-back covers days 1156–1161 by their index titles and carries (those scripts were not on disk when this was written). Karimah al-Marwaziyyah is named by first name only.
